task: How much more explanatory power does the discrete finite-history replay provide over the generic continuous first-order theory?

protocol.gradient_sequence: Same real paired {G_t^1.0, G_t^1.3}_{t=1..20} from the frozen #49 Arm-A checkpoints (k32/k64/k128/k256, same seed-3 trajectory)
protocol.starting_point: UNIFORM fresh start (m0=0, v0=0, step0=0) for all three predictors, so the first-order formula is complete (the full history is the 20-step gradient history; the real extracted state would encode pre-checkpoint history the first-order formula cannot see)

predictors.scalar: a*_j = <G^g_j,G_j>/||G_j||^2; Ghat_j = a*_j G_j; replay RAdam -> h^scalar = replay(Ghat)/u1
predictors.firstorder: delta_j = a*_j - 1; A^(1) = (sum beta1^{t-j} delta_j G_j)/(sum beta1^{t-j} G_j); A^(2) = (sum beta2^{t-j} delta_j G_j^2)/(sum beta2^{t-j} G_j^2); h^firstorder = 1 + A^(1) - A^(2)
predictors.replay: h^replay = replay(G^g)/u1 (exact moment recursion, the reference)

protocol.effective_support: top 1% of coords by |u1| (np.partition quantile mask)

validation.replay: pure-numpy float32 RAdam (analysis/numpy_radam.py), validated against stored torch histories to ~1 ulp (cross-K verify_u1_final)
validation.synthetic_smoke: local synthetic near-scalar test passed before server run
validation.firstorder_formula: incremental exponential-sum recurrence verified against the closed form
